newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy privatisations mustn't exclude market - Consob.
newsitem.headline: Italy privatisations mustn't exclude market - Consob.

text.p: The control of privatised Italian companies should not be protected by measures which limit the role of the stock market, Italian Bourse regulator Consob said.
Referring to recent sell-offs, Consob said it approved the principle of stable shareholding cores as long as these did not signify an unlimited guarantee of the maintenance of control.

"To increase the efficiency of the financial market and to protect minority shareholders, it is desirable that the stable cores, or other forms of shareholding agreement, should be created in such a way as to make it possible for control to be contested," it said.

Consob noted that privatisations could be carried out either by a straight public sale offer (OPV) or by resorting to direct negotiation with potential buyers for private placements, or both at the same time.

If a public offer was accompanied by sale accords with shareholders themselves tied by control agreements and such accords were made public prior to the sale, then no successive or unforeseen changes to arrangements for the original launch of the public offer were likely, Consob said.

"But such an arrangement reduces the possibility that controlling coalitions could be formed following share buying on the market and that the Bourse could have a role in the allocation of controlling rights, which would in fact be desirable," it said.

Furthermore, it remained to be evaluated "whether the continuation in the statutes of privatised companies of share holding limits did not constitute a serious obstacle to the efficacy of the privatisation procedures in the periods following the placements," Consob added.
It said privatisations were an important factor in stock market growth, particularly in countries where the ratio of bourse capitalisation to gross domestic product was relatively limited.
In France, the value of public sale offers for privatisations carried out between 1993 and 1996 equalled some 5.5 percent of bourse capitalisation.

In smaller markets like those of Italy and Spain, the contribution of privatisations to the growth of the equity market was higher, equal to some 10 percent for Italy and around seven percent for Spain.
Consob noted that Italian privatisations carried out through the market since 1993 amounted to a value of over 30 trillion lire.
